newsitem.title: GERMANY: BDI head expects Germany to meet EMU deficit goal.
newsitem.headline: BDI head expects Germany to meet EMU deficit goal.

text.p: Hans-Olaf Henkel, president of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), said on Wednesday he expects Germany will keep its budget deficit below 3.0 percent of economic output this year in keeping with guidelines for participation in European monetary union (EMU).
Asked in a radio interview whether he shared the government's optimism that it could hold the deficit to 2.9 percent, Henkel said, "I have no reason not to share it.
"2.9 percent is a bit of a close shave, and the economy is at the moment not especially convincing, but there are still opportunities for the government to do something."
The government is also discussing more austerity measures, but it must take care to cut consumption without trimming investment, Henkel said.
Bonn's planned tax reform could also have a positive symbolic effect, and greater flexibility on the labour market would also help, he said.
The current weakness of the mark could be a big boost for German exports, the current dynamo of the economy, he said.

State secretary for finance Juergen Stark this week defended the 2.9 percent deficit projection, saying it took account of all recognised risks, and was not threatened even by the sharp jump in January unemployment to a new postwar record.
Henkel conceded that not all economic risks could be recognised, as the past two years show. But he said the government had a realistic view of the labour market.
He also said he favoured a strict interpretation of the criteria, for political rather than economic reasons.

"Many (German) politicians have been hectoring our partners for years about strict adherence to the convergence criteria," he said. "So we are now in the weakest position to say ... we can afford to be lax."
He noted that the countries that have had the greatest success in bolstering their jobs markets in recent years -- including Britain and the U.S. have had stringent economic policies.
Portugal is likely to meet the EMU criteria, while Spain and Italy have shown great progress
"One thing we should keep in mind: currency union is coming. The parliaments have decided, entire nations have been polled, constitutions have been changed. Of that there is no doubt," he said.
Henkel said he also shares the government view that countries' progress in meeting the convergence criteria should determine the start date for EMU, and not the other way around.
